<!--

-->

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Fix ReplicaSet deletion rank for multiple colocation nodes.

#### Which issue(s) this PR fixes:
<!--
*Automatically closes linked issue when PR is merged.
Usage: `Fixes #<issue number>`, or `Fixes (paste link of issue)`.
_If PR is about `failing-tests or flakes`, please post the related issues/tests in a comment and do not use `Fixes`_*
-->
Fixes #102948 

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

Now for a ReplicaSet or Deployment which has five Pods on two Nodes:

```
node01: pod-a, pod-b, pod-c
node02: pod-d, pod-e
```

When replicas changed from `5` to `2`, the deletion rank that controller will get for Pods:

```
node01:
- pod-a: 3
- pod-b: 3
- pod-c: 3
node02:
- pod-d: 2
- pod-e: 2
```

So ReplicaSet will choose all three Pods on `node01` to delete.

This PR fixes the rank to be:

```
node01:
- pod-a: 3
- pod-b: 2
- pod-c: 1
node02:
- pod-d: 2
- pod-e: 1
```

So that controller will delete Pods more evenly.

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

-->
No user-facing changed.

/sig apps

issue_context.title: [Bug] ReplicaSet incorrect deletion rank when there are multiple colocation nodes
issue_context.body:
<!-- Please use this template while reporting a bug and provide as much info as possible. Not doing so may result in your bug not being addressed in a timely manner. Thanks!

If the matter is security related, please disclose it privately via https://kubernetes.io/security/
-->


#### What happened:
When ReplicaSet prepares to delete Pods, it will calculate the rank of Pods by same node  spread.

Now here are two Nodes and five Pods on them:

```
node01: pod-a, pod-b, pod-c
node02: pod-d, pod-e
```

Then modify the replicas from `5` to `2`, ReplicaSet will delete all three Pods on `node01` and leave two Pods running on `node02`.

It is because the rank of the three Pods on `node01` are all `3`, and the rank of the two Pods on `node02` are `2`. So controller sort the Pods by rank and choose the first three Pods with rank `3` to delete.

#### What you expected to happen:

In this case, ReplicaSet should delete two Pods on `node01` and one Pod on `node02`.

#### How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible):

1. create a ReplicaSet or Deployment with `replicas=5` onto 2 Nodes
2. ensure all Pods spread on Nodes, and wait them running and ready
3. change replicas to `2`

/sig apps

review_comments:
I think what you had before (fixed dates, close to each other) made more sense as a fair comparison.

We have two competing heuristics:
1. Removing the youngest pods, as they are likely to have less usage 
2. Keeping the spread

My proposal is giving some priority to 1, but when this is equal, it will try to keep 2.

Your proposal is giving priority to 2, but when this is equal, it will keep 1.

Since your test is giving random timestamps, my proposal wont behave like yours, because it's optimizing for different things. If you keep the timestamps close to each other, they should behave very similar.

Now comes the question: which heuristic is more important, time or spread? I think my proposal gives a good balance between both. Your proposal favors 2 regardless of timestamps.

@kow3ns @soltysh any thoughts?
@FillZpp are you still working on this?
Yes, but I'm not sure what else I can do for this...
What are your thoughts on my proposal after the last explanation?
Were you able to test just removing the ranks?

Yeah, I used to test it without ranks. Turns out the random algorithm could not choose the expected pods that should have been deleted according to SameNode policy.

However, it was tested in my tiny kind cluster. The random algorithm might work better in production cluster, in which pods should be more randomize.

The current implementation still has the ranks. Do you think it's worth to change this PR to remove the ranks?

Re-iterating on what I said earlier:

You should fix the dates, otherwise the algorithm would prioritize removing the oldest pods first.

> If you keep the timestamps close to each other, they should behave very similar.

Emm.. I can do this in unit-test. But how can we ensure the timestamps of all pods are close in production? The pods were probably scaled up in different time and by different ppl, e.g., manually, HPA.

They might not be close in production. And that's when the age criteria will take precedence.

But when all conditions are equal, it would will be completely random.

Note that the timestamps are compared in a logarithmic fashion. Pod A is only consider older than Pod B if it has been running for at least twice the time. Otherwise they are considered equal.

I can take an example that we have generally observed in production.

Once there is an application that has deployed for some days. It has several pods scheduled on the same node because of the limited resource when it scaled up.
Now we add some new nodes into the cluster and we have to migrate the colocated pods to the new nodes. So we are going to increase the `replicas` to create several pods, wait them to be ready, and then decrease the `replicas` and hoping Deployment delete the colocated pods. However, it will probably delete the pods we have just created.

You may ask why not just delete the colocated pods and let controller create new pods and schedule to the new nodes. It is because we have to guarantee the number of ready pods to protect availability for applications.

I think a migration use case needs an explicit API, rather than toying with the number of replicas.

In a way, it is similar to a rollout, except that in this case you are upgrading/stopping a node.

The first step is cordoning a node. But then you want the replicaset controller to create a new pod before the old pod is deleted.

Can you join the next SIG meeting to discuss this?

> Can you join the next SIG meeting to discuss this?

Sure, I would like to. Besides, this case is just one of the various conditions in production. My point is the timestamps of pods are probably complicated and may be far more than "twice the time". So as you said, what we have to choose is keeping the spread strictly or removing the younger pods which may possibly keep the spread in some cases.
This function doesn't sort with logarithmic comparisons

In my opinion, there is no need to sort pods on the same node with logarithmic comparisons, which are designed to solve the sort problem across different topologies (such as multiple failure domains).

The pods on different nodes that have the same rank will be sort by logarithmic in the later ActivePodsWithRanks.
